stops.title: Huygens' principle, reflection & refraction
stops.inShort: Every point on a wavefront acts as a secondary source emitting secondary wavelets. The forward envelope gives the new wavefront. Used to prove laws of reflection (i = r) and Snell's law (sin i / sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁).

stops.title: Polarization & Brewster's law
stops.inShort: Polarization proves the transverse nature of light. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ. Brewster's law: at polarizing angle θ_B, reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular and tan θ_B = n₂/n₁.

stops.title: Interference & Young's double slit experiment (YDSE)
stops.inShort: Constructive interference: path difference Δx = nλ; destructive: Δx = (2n−1)λ/2. Fringe width β = λD/d (constant for all bright and dark fringes). Coherent sources have constant phase difference.

stops.title: Diffraction of light at a single slit
stops.inShort: Bending of light around edges of an obstacle/aperture. For Fraunhofer single-slit diffraction (slit width a), minima occur at a sin θ = nλ; width of central maximum = 2λD/a.
sections: 7.9.3 Fraunhofer Diffraction at a Single Slit

stops.title: Resolving power of microscope & telescope
stops.inShort: Rayleigh's criterion: two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other. Microscope RP = 1/d_min = 2n sin θ / λ; Telescope RP = 1/dθ = D / (1.22 λ).

items.s: At θ_B, reflected ray is completely plane polarized.
Path difference at distance y from centre: Δx = y d / D.

board.text: What is Brewster's law? Derive the formula for Brewster's angle.
board.answer:
Brewster's law: The tangent of the polarizing angle (Brewster's angle θ_B) for a transparent medium is equal to its refractive index (tan θ_B = n₂/n₁).
Derivation: When unpolarized light is incident at θ_B, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other: θ_B + r + 90° = 180° ⇒ r = 90° − θ_B.
By Snell's law: n₁ sin θ_B = n₂ sin r = n₂ sin(90° − θ_B) = n₂ cos θ_B.
Therefore tan θ_B = n₂ / n₁.

board.text: Derive laws of reflection of light using Huygens' principle.
board.answer:
Consider a plane wavefront AB incident at angle i on a plane reflecting surface MN. As A touches MN, secondary wavelet from A spreads in the same medium with speed c while B reaches C in time t (BC = ct).
Draw a hemisphere of radius AE = ct from A and tangent plane EC.
In right ΔABC and ΔAEC: AC is common, AE = BC = ct, ∠ABC = ∠AEC = 90°.
Hence ΔABC ≅ ΔAEC ⇒ ∠BAC = ∠ECA, i.e., angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r. Incident ray, normal, and reflected ray lie in the same plane.

points.text: Wavefront diagram and secondary wavelet radius AE = BC = ct

board.text: Obtain an expression for fringe width in Young's double slit experiment.
board.answer:
Let two coherent slits S₁, S₂ separated by d be at distance D from screen (D >> d).
At point P at distance y from central point O: S₂P² − S₁P² = [D² + (y + d/2)²] − [D² + (y − d/2)²] = 2 y d.
Since S₂P + S₁P ≈ 2D, path difference Δx = S₂P − S₁P ≈ y d / D.
For nth bright fringe: y_n = n λ D / d.
Fringe width β = y_{n+1} − y_n = λ D / d.

board.text: Distinguish between interference and diffraction of light (any four points).
board.answer:
1. Interference is due to superposition of waves from two distinct coherent sources; diffraction is due to superposition of secondary wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront.
2. All bright fringes in interference have equal intensity; in diffraction, intensity decreases rapidly away from central maximum.
3. Fringe width is constant in interference; central maximum is twice as wide as secondary maxima in diffraction.
4. Dark fringes are usually completely dark in interference; minima are never perfectly dark in diffraction.
